messages.subject: program Distance vs distsamp estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi I was wondering if someone could shed some light on differences in
density and detection probability between program Distance and the
distsamp function. I ran some analysis for ovenbird in Program
DISTANCE where I get a density of 10 birds/km sq., detection p 64% and
with the distsamp function I get density estimates of 18 birds/km sq.
detection p 36%.  I think the difference in detection probability is
causing this discrepancy. I am also using the same distance bins and
detection function.
I don't expect the density estimates to be the same but I thought that
they should be somewhat closer.  Any ideas on how I can figure out
what my be causing the difference in detection probability.

thanks,
Rob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

I made the comparison again with simulated point transect data and the half-normal detection function, and the results are the same:

                    density       sigma
    Truth          15.00         25.00
    unmarked   14.23         25.18
    DISTANCE 14.23         25.18

The R code (lifted from unmarked's unitTests) is below. My suspicion is that the discrepancy you found has to do with specifying either "AREA" or "EFFORT" in DISTANCE. For example, did you specify how much area was surveyed (including points with no detections)? I would check that and then try ignoring the EFFORT option.

Please let us know if you get to the bottom of this.

Richard

Simulation code:

simPt <- function(lambda=5, sigma=20, npts=100,
    breaks=seq(0, 50, by=10))
{
    radius <- max(breaks)
    A <- (2*radius)^2 / 10000 # Area (ha) of square containing circle
    y1 <- numeric(0)
    pt <- character(0)
    y2 <- matrix(NA, npts, length(breaks)-1)
    labs <- c(letters, paste(letters, letters, sep=""))
    for(i in 1:npts) {
        M <- rpois(1, lambda * A) # Individuals within the square
        # coordinates of each individual
        xy <- cbind(x=runif(M, -radius, radius), y=runif(M, -radius, radius))

        # Distances from each point
        d <- apply(xy, 1, function(x) sqrt(x[1]^2 + x[2]^2))
        d <- d[d <= radius]

        # Detection process
        if(length(d)) {
            p <- exp(-d^2 / (2 * sigma^2)) # half-normal
            d <- d[rbinom(length(d), 1, p) == 1]
            y1 <- c(y1, d)
            pt <- c(pt, rep(labs[i], length(d)))
            y2[i,] <- table(cut(d, breaks, include.lowest=TRUE))
            }
        }
    return(list(y1=data.frame(pt, y1), y2=y2))
}

set.seed(3)

db <- seq(0, 50, by=10)

sim1 <- simPt(15, 25, 50,db)
str(sim1)

nrow(sim1$y1) == sum(sim1$y2) # Should be true

library(unmarked)

umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y=sim1$y2, dist.breaks=db, survey="point", unitsIn="m")

(m1 <- distsamp(~1~1, umf))
exp(coef(m1)) # D=14.23371, sigma=25.177

write.table(sim1$y1, "sim1.txt", row.names=F, sep=",")

messages.subject: Is Unmarked calculating AICc or AIC?
messages.subject_clean: Is Unmarked calculating AICc or AIC?
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I decided to run my single-species, multi-season occupancy models
in Unmarked after running them in a different software package. I
think the Unmarked package is a lot easier to work in, but after
running the models in Unmarked, I noticed Unmarked is calculating AICc
not AIC. I looked at previous threads on the google group, and I did
not notice any resolution on this issue. It’s not a big deal, I can
calculate either AICc or AIC given the -2log and number of parameters.
But what is it calculating; the output calls it AIC?
The example below is from when I run a constant model and a “habitat”
model with n=47. Notice that 261.5+(2*4) does not equal 270.5 (it
equals 269.5) but when we account for the 47 sites and calculate AICc,
261.5+2*4(47/(47-4-1) , we get 270.452380… which is very similar to
the AIC value in the table. This is even clearer when there are more
parameters (habitat model). I have double checked this table to model@
AIC and I get the same results.

                                          Model Converge -2logLik K
AIC DeltaAIC     w
1 ~habitat , ~habitat , ~habitat , ~1        0   -249.8      7
266.7      0.0 0.869
2                   ~1 , ~1 , ~1 , ~1              0   -261.5      4
270.5      3.8 0.131

Chad Hockenbary
GRA

fmAIC <- 2 * opt$value + 2 * nP + 2*nP*(nP + 1)/(M - nP - 1)

which I guess is AICc assuming that the sample size is equal to the number of sites. I will fix this so that it returns AIC to be
consistent with the other fitting functions. In the meantime, note that you can get the log likelihood by typing:

logLik(someModel)

Richard

Best,
Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel,

Although this appears to be a bug, I think the real problem relates to
the use of the delta method when you are near a parameter boundary.
What happens is that the SE of the beta coefficient is usually very
high when you are near a boundary, but the back-transformed SE can be
very small. As for the backtransformed CI, unmarked ensures that it is
constrained to the appropriate domain by working with the SE from the
beta estimates. That is why you see the discrepancy. The associated
code is here https://github.com/rbchan/unmarked/blob/master/R/unmarkedLinComb.R.

So, possible options are:

1. Use CI = Est +/- 1.96*SE and realize that the CI may not be
properly constrained
2. Use "nonparboot" or "parboot".
3. Become a Bayesian so that you don't have to worry about these approximations!

Option 2 is probably best if you have the time.

Richard

In this case, I would suggest using a non-parametric bootstrap

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

On the distsamp help page, under "Note", it says "you cannot use
obsCovs." In the distance sampling context, obsCovs are
distance-interval-specific covariates, and I'm not sure if how the
model would perform with that type of covariate. Maybe Andy can weigh
in about this. If the model does work in this case, perhaps I should
make it possible to include obsCovs.

As for cluster size, you are right that you could simply estimate the
density of clusters and then multiply by the mean cluster size.
However, you would probably want to determine if detection probability
is affected by cluster size. The only way I can think of to do that
with this model would require that a maximum of 1 cluster was detected
in each "cell" of your y matrix. Then you could use cluster size as a
distance interval-specific-covariate (assuming this is possible).

I should add functions to return effective strip half-width and
effective area. Until then you can do it manually using the formulas
found in Buckland et al. 2001. The first example on the help page is
for line transects and yields an estimate of 10.9 for the half-normal
shape parameter. The maximum distance is 20, so effective strip
half-width is

integrate(gxhn, 0, 20, sigma=10.9)$value # =12.75m
12.75/20 # = 0.64 is the detection probability

For the point-transect example, the shape parameter estimate is 9.8
and effective area is

grhn <- function(r, sigma)  exp(-r^2/(2*sigma^2)) * r
2*pi * integrate(grhn, 0, 25, sigma=9.8)$value # = 580 m^2
580/(pi*25^2) # = 0.30 is the detection probability

Thanks for your questions. Hope this helps.

Richard

For example:

fm <- colext(psiformula=~1, gammaformula=~x1, epsilonformula=~x1,

soon.

predict(fm, type="col") # or type="ext"

plogis(model.matrix(~x1, site.covs) %*% coef(fm, type="col"))

oc <- obsCovs(yourUMF)
X <- model.matrix(~cov1 + cov2 + etc..., oc) # design matrix
betas <- coef(yourFittedModel, type="det")
p <- plogis(X %*% betas)

If you want SEs and CIs, you could apply the delta method yourself, or use either nonparboot or parboot.

Hope this helps,
Richard
